articles.summary: Year-end payroll preparation in Nigeria carries extra weight this December. 2026 was the first full year under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, so the figures you close with cover a year in which the PAYE rules changed while payroll was running: the Consolidated Relief Allowance gave way to a ₦800,000 zero-rate band and rent relief. Your system has probably run consistently all year. The review tells you whether it ran correctly. This guide follows the 9 checks that bring payroll, bank and accounting records into agreement before the employer annual return falls due on 31 January, and points to where errors tend to sit: the transition months, undocumented reliefs, pension credits that never reached a Retirement Savings Account, and headcount that differs between HR and payroll. What Is Year-End Payroll Preparation? Year-end payroll preparation is the work of reconciling a full year of payroll against bank and accounting records, confirming that statutory contributions were handled correctly, and closing the year with figures you can support, before the employer’s annual return is filed. Three terms get used interchangeably, and each catches a different kind of error. Payroll Reconciliation Matching payroll reports to bank payments and ledger entries. Our guide to payroll reconciliation in Nigeria explains this further. Payroll Audit Reviewing the process behind the numbers: who can change a salary, who approves a run, and which controls exist. See our guide to payroll audit in Nigeria. Payroll Year-End Closing Locking the records and producing the figures for the employer annual return and for the first payroll of January. Why Nigerian Businesses Should Complete a Year-End Payroll Review The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 took effect on 1 January 2026, so the review should also cover how the new rules were applied month by month, including any weeks when payroll settings were still being updated. Finding those cases now lets you correct them in the December run, ahead of the 31 January return. Done properly, the review also confirms that salary calculations are right, employee payment records are complete, deductions and remittances agree, and outstanding liabilities and bonuses are documented. That is what your annual return and your year-end accounts rest on. Year-End Payroll Preparation Checklist for Nigerian Businesses 1. Review Employee Information and Payroll Records Start with a headcount: opening headcount plus hires minus exits should equal closing headcount in HR records, in payroll and on the pension schedule. Then check each file for tax ID, start and exit dates, department, salary structure, bank details and allowances, and match every salary change to a signed approval. Records work is dull, but it is where the rest of the review starts. 2. Reconcile Monthly Salary Payments Lay your 12 payroll reports beside the bank statements. Net salary on the report should equal what left the account, and gross pay, overtime, arrears and corrected entries should each trace to a record. A gap of ₦40,000 can be a reversed payment, a duplicate, or a manual transfer that never reached the payroll system. Set a variance rule while you are at it. Pick a percentage, for example 5%, and investigate any employee whose net pay moved by more than that between months without an approved change. 3. Review PAYE Tax Calculations and Remittances PAYE has the most moving parts this year, here are 4 checks: Transition months. Find the first payroll cycle in which your system applied the new rules. If the old relief logic stayed live for even one run, or relief inputs were loaded late, those employees were taxed differently from everyone else. Recompute each employee’s full-year PAYE under the new rules, compare it with PAYE deducted from January to November plus the projected December amount, and sort the differences by size. A few large ones usually share a single cause. Agree the correction method with your tax adviser and the relevant state revenue service before touching payslips. December bonuses. Rebuild the December PAYE for three bonus recipients, once cumulatively for the year to date and once for December alone. If your system’s figure matches neither, the configuration needs fixing. If it matches December alone, expect sharp drops in net pay and queries in January. Rent relief coverage. Rent relief is 20% of annual rent paid, capped at ₦500,000, and the Joint Revenue Board’s 2026 guidelines expect the tenant’s name, rent paid and period covered, the property address, and the landlord’s details. Track one ratio: employees with documents on file divided by employees with relief applied. Where it falls below 100%, apply each person’s marginal rate to the undocumented relief to see the tax at stake, then either collect the paperwork or withdraw the relief in the December run. Deducted versus remitted. Monthly PAYE goes to the State Internal Revenue Service, and states generally work to the 10th of the following month. List each employee’s state of work beside the state you remitted to, since remote and relocated staff are where mismatches turn up, then compare deductions with remittances month by month. Each remittance reference becomes a line in the annual return. Our guide to the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 and payroll explains. 4. Verify National Housing Fund (NHF) Contributions NHF is mandatory for public sector employees and voluntary for private sector staff under the Business Facilitation Act, so every private-sector deduction needs the employee’s consent on file, and a deduction without it gets refunded. Identify who is covered or has opted in, match deductions and confirm the contribution basis before building a calculation, against current Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria guidance. 5. Review NSITF Contributions The Employees’ Compensation Scheme covers workers injured, disabled or made ill by their jobs, and the employer funds it entirely. NSITF puts the contribution at 1% of total monthly payroll, so a ₦10,000,000 payroll produces ₦100,000 a month and ₦1,200,000 across the year. articles.summary: You clip a fresh target to the carrier, send it out to seven yards and settle into your stance. Two lanes over, another shooter starts working through a box of 9mm, and the sound of every one of those shots comes back at you off the concrete walls. By the end of your hour, your ears feel full and the drive home sounds a little muffled. That full, muffled feeling is a sign that the one layer of hearing protection you were wearing wasn't enough for a closed room. If you're choosing between earplugs and earmuffs, the best indoor range ear protection is both: earplugs seated under earmuffs. According to NIOSH, earmuffs alone cut peak gunshot noise by an average of 26 dB, while earmuffs worn over earplugs cut it by 44 dB. NIOSH recommends double protection at indoor firing ranges. Electronic earmuffs let you wear both layers of hearing protection and still hear range commands. If you're planning your first trip to the range, it's easier to start with both layers than to add one later. Your situation Earplugs, earmuffs or both Why A one-hour handgun session in a lane Both: foam earplugs under passive or electronic earmuffs NIOSH recommends double protection at indoor ranges A class or private lesson Both: earplugs under electronic earmuffs Hear-through carries your instructor's voice without lifting a cup A rifle at an indoor bench Both: earplugs under slim, low-profile electronic earmuffs Slim cups leave room for your cheek weld A lane next to a muzzle brake or compensator Both, and consider asking for a different lane Brakes and compensators push blast sideways toward neighboring lanes A full day as an instructor or RSO Both: comfortable earplugs under long-runtime electronic earmuffs Your exposure adds up across every relay you run Indoor Ranges Reflect Every Gunshot Sound Back at You The ringing in your ears after an indoor shooting session happens because of how a closed room handles sound. Outdoors, the sound blast from your firearm spreads out over open ground. Indoors, your range's concrete walls, ceiling, baffles, and lane dividers reflect that blast back toward the firing line. A gunshot is already over the noise safe limit before any reflection adds to it. NIOSH measured peak sound pressure levels of 155 to 168 dB SPL from law enforcement firearms during live fire. The limit for impulse noise is 140 dB peak, and OSHA's noise standard sets that same ceiling. Every 10 dB is ten times the sound energy, so a shot that lands 28 dB over the limit carries several hundred times the energy the limit allows. Reflected sound can reach your ears a fraction of a second after the direct sound. You hear your muzzle blast first, and then the room sends part of that blast sound back to you. Those same walls reflect the shots from every other lane too. A shooter three lanes down is firing into the same room you are, and you have no say over how many rounds that shooter fires. Muzzle brakes and compensators can make that sound worse at close range. A muzzle brake on a rifle or a compensator on a pistol vents gas out the sides of the muzzle. That side blast hits the lane dividers and pushes toward the shooters beside it, so a braked rifle at the bench next to you can be the loudest firearm you hear in your session. A lane rental often means an hour of steady fire, so your exposure keeps adding up long after shooting your first magazine. Sound source Outdoor range Indoor range Your own muzzle blast Spreads out over open ground Reflects off walls, ceiling, and baffles Shooters in nearby lanes Often spaced farther apart Lanes a few feet apart, firing into the same walls Braked rifles and compensated pistols Side blast disperses into open air Side blast hits lane dividers and stays in the room An hour of continuous fire Sound carries away from the line Every shot in the hour reflects back toward the line You can read about how many decibels a gunshot is for common calibers in our gunshot decibel guide. All of that reflected sound lands on your earplugs first. The next section shows why a single earplug can't handle it. Why Earplugs Alone Aren't Enough at an Indoor Range Earplugs alone aren't sufficient hearing protection on an indoor shooting range because a single layer can leave the loudest gunshots above the 140 dB peak limit. NIOSH measured an average peak reduction of 24 dB for earplugs alone. Against a 168 dB shot, that still leaves about 144 dB at your ear. NIOSH's case data shows how much a second layer adds: Setup Average peak reduction (NIOSH case data) A 168 dB shot at your ear Earplugs alone 24 dB About 144 dB, over the limit Earmuffs alone 26 dB About 142 dB, over the limit Earplugs under earmuffs 44 dB About 124 dB, under the limit The combined 44 dB is lower than the two layers added together, which would be 50 dB. One reason for this is that some sound reaches your inner ear through the bones of your skull, and no earplug or earmuff blocks that path. Even so, the second layer is what brings a 168 dB shot under the 140 dB limit. A higher-rated earplug won't close that gap by itself. The Noise Reduction Rating (NRR) on your earplug packaging comes from lab testing with a careful fit. At the range, a rushed insertion or an ear tip in the wrong size can loosen the seal into your ear canal and cost you a large share of that rated protection. You can learn how NRR ratings work, and how to estimate your real-world protection, in our NRR guide. You'll see two ratings on AXIL products. NRR is the rating required on hearing protection sold in the United States. The Single Number Rating (SNR) comes from European testing, and a product's SNR usually reads a few decibels higher than its NRR. Compare NRR to NRR and SNR to SNR when you shop. For an indoor range, plan on wearing two layers of hearing protection. Earplugs under earmuffs will protect you better indoors than one device with a higher number on the box. Two passive layers give you that protection, but two passive layers also make range commands hard to hear. Electronic earmuffs solve that problem. Best Electronic Ear Protection for Indoor Shooting Ranges The best electronic ear protection for an indoor shooting range is a pair of electronic earmuffs worn over passive earplugs. That setup gives you NIOSH's recommended two layers of hearing protection and keeps range commands clear. With two passive layers on, it's hard to hear the range safety officer, a cease-fire call or the instructor standing behind you. When you can't hear a command, the natural move is to lift one earmuff cup. If someone fires while that cup is up, that ear is down to one layer of protection or none. Electronic earmuffs remove the reason to lift a cup. The microphones on your electronic earmuffs pick up speech and range commands and play them through the earmuff speakers. The earmuff circuit clamps down the instant a gunshot crosses its threshold, and your earplugs hold the seal underneath. That's the Protect + Enhance idea behind AXIL's electronic earmuffs: block the harmful noise and amplify the low-level sounds you still need. When you compare electronic earmuffs for an indoor range, four features do most of the work: Feature Why it helps indoors What to look for Compression circuit Reflected gunshots arrive back to back from every lane A circuit that clamps down the instant a gunshot crosses its threshold Hear-through volume Your earplugs muffle speech under the cups Enough volume steps to make up for the earplug layer Low-profile cups Rifle stocks and bench positions crowd your earmuffs Slim cups that clear your cheek weld Runtime Lane sessions can run an hour or more, and range days run longer A full session or day on one charge or one set of batteries One thing to look out for is an electronic earmuff circuit's reaction speed. A slow circuit can let the start of each gunshot through before it clamps down. Electronic earbuds can also take the place of passive earplugs as your inner layer. Before a long session, check that your earbuds sit flush enough for your earmuff cushions to seal over them comfortably. An electronic setup only protects you as well as it fits. Seat your earplugs first, then put on your earmuffs, so the earmuff cushions close over your sealed ear canals. Tip: Roll your foam earplug tips tight, pull the top of your ear up and back, and hold each earplug in place for a few seconds while the foam expands. Shooting glasses with thin, flat arms let your earmuff cushions seal around the arms with a smaller gap. Tip: Put your glasses on before your earmuffs, then press each earmuff cushion flat against the glasses arm. A lane customer only needs that electronic setup to stay comfortable for an hour. Range safety officers and firearms instructors need the same setup to last the whole day. Hearing Protection for Range Safety Officers and Firearms Instructors Range safety officers and firearms instructors should consider wearing comfortable earplugs under long-runtime electronic earmuffs that they can wear for every relay of the day. Your exposure is far higher than any customer's, so your hearing protection has to do more. A customer fires one session, while the person running the line hears every session, every day. Hearing damage from gunfire builds up across all of that exposure, which our article on shooter's ear explains in more detail. NIOSH reports that lead and noise at firing ranges can cause health problems, particularly among employees and instructors. Many firearms instructors also train law enforcement. On qualification day, a whole unit can cycle through your lanes, often with rifles and shotguns alongside pistols. NIOSH's double-protection recommendation applies to the instructor running that line as much as to the officers on it. For all-day wear, look for electronic earmuffs that run a full day on one charge, low-profile cups that stay comfortable for hours, and replaceable cushions for gear that sees heavy or shared use. Pair those earmuffs with an earplug you can wear for hours without noticing it. The MX PRO earmuffs run up to 70 hours in hearing enhancement mode, which covers several full range days between charges. Electronic hear-through lets you give commands and hear shooters' questions without lifting a cup. If radio communication is part of your job on the line, our comparison of tactical headsets and tactical earbuds covers the options built for that. For duty gear, you can browse AXIL's law enforcement hearing protection. Tip: Before the first relay, do a voice check with both layers of hearing protection on. Have a partner stand one lane away and call commands at normal volume, then raise your earmuff volume until you can follow every word. Setting the volume before shooting starts means you won't be reaching for a dial with a loaded firearm in your hand. Best Ear Muffs and Earplugs for Indoor Shooting Ranges The best ear muffs and earplugs for an indoor shooting range are a pair you'll wear together. Earplugs under earmuffs give you more protection indoors than any single device. Are earplugs enough for the range? At an outdoor range with a handgun, well-fitted earplugs may be enough for a short session. At an indoor range, NIOSH recommends earplugs and earmuffs together. Do noise cancelling headphones work at a gun range? Consumer noise cancelling headphones only count as hearing protection if they carry an NRR. Our article on noise cancelling earbuds at the range explains why active noise cancellation can't stop the sound of a gunshot. How loud is a gunshot indoors? Do gun ranges provide ear protection? Most ranges rent or sell basic passive hearing protection. Bringing your own lets you choose the fit and add the second layer. What should range safety officers and instructors wear? Range safety officers and instructors should consider comfortable earplugs under long-runtime electronic earmuffs, so commands carry without anyone lifting a cup. If you're starting from one pair of earmuffs, begin with a pack of earplugs to wear under them. When you're ready to upgrade, electronic earmuffs let you hear the line without lifting a cup. Before you leave your house, pack both layers of hearing protection with your range bag essentials, and charge your electronic earmuffs or pack spare batteries. At your lane, seat your earplugs, put on your earmuffs and set your hear-through volume with a quick voice check. On the firing line, leave both layers on until you've stepped back. If you need to hear someone, raise your earmuff volume instead of lifting a cup. When you're done shooting, wash up and wipe down your hearing protection before you eat. By lunch, the earplug has worked itself loose without you noticing, and the press you stopped hearing hours ago is suddenly the loudest thing in the room. That's the difficulty with picking industrial hearing protection off a spec sheet. The Noise Reduction Rating (NRR) on the package is a lab figure measured with a careful fit. OSHA's guidance subtracts 7 dB from that rating and, in some cases, cuts what's left in half. A hearing protector can look adequate on paper and still leave you over the limit, so choosing well means starting from your measured noise level and planning for fit, comfort, and the need to hear the people around you. Know Your Plant's Noise Exposure Before You Pick a Hearing Protector Before you compare a single hearing protector equipment, you have to find out how loud your area of the plant gets. Every method for judging a protector, from OSHA's to NIOSH's, starts from one number: your work area's noise level averaged over an 8-hour day. That figure is the time-weighted average (TWA). An NRR can't tell you anything useful until you know your TWA. OSHA's noise standard draws two lines. At an 85 dBA TWA, also called the action level, your employer has to run a hearing conservation program. At 90 dBA, the permissible exposure limit (PEL), hearing protection is required for all workers in that area. OSHA's rule also says your hearing protectors must bring your noise exposure level down to at least 90 dBA, and down to 85 dBA if your annual hearing test has already shown a significant drop in your hearing. That lower 85 dBA target is easy to overlook, and it raises the bar for anyone whose hearing has already slipped. For the full rule, including who has to provide protection and when, see our guide to OSHA hearing protection requirements. Noise levels vary a lot from one area of your plant to the next. Your own area's TWA comes from your employer's noise monitoring, which is part of a hearing conservation program. For a fuller chart of everyday and industrial sound levels, see our article on what dB level requires ear protection. Tip: If you don't know your area's TWA, ask your safety lead or supervisor. A phone app gives you a spot reading of one moment, and a TWA covers your whole workday. Once you know your number, the next decision is which hearing protector type you'll actually keep in for that whole workday. Industrial Earplugs, Earmuffs, and Earbuds Compared for the Plant Floor Your TWA tells you how much protection you need. The form factor of hearing protections decide how much of the labeled rating you get on an ordinary day at work, so it's worth comparing earplugs, earmuffs, and electronic earbuds side by side. Industrial Earplugs: High Lab Ratings, Wide Real-World Spread Foam earplugs carry some of the highest lab ratings on the shelf. Foam also shows the widest spread in real-world results, because the protection depends on how well you roll and insert each earplug. A shallow fit can cost you much of the rating, and a pre-molded earplug in the wrong size can leak in the same way. You can learn how to compare materials and sizes in our guide to choosing earplugs for work. Industrial Earmuffs: The Most Consistent Fit Earmuffs seal around your ear instead of inside it, so the fit varies less from one worker to the next. A supervisor can also see at a glance whether your industrial earmuffs are on. But earmuffs are the weakest option with thick safety glasses on your temples, a hot floor, and hard hats that aren't built to work with them. Electronic Earbuds and Earmuffs: Protection That Keeps Speech Audible Electronic hearing protection follows AXIL's Protect + Enhance approach. A microphone and circuit compresses loud machine noises to protect your ears while amplifying lower-level sounds like speech, backup alarms, and a machine changing pitch. On a long day, that awareness can decide whether your protection stays in or comes out. Electronic earbuds also add a slim fit that works with safety glasses. How the Three Types Compare on the Floor Each form factor trades protection, comfort, and awareness differently: Foam or pre-molded earplugs Passive earmuffs Electronic earbuds Electronic earmuffs Real-world consistency Lowest, depends on insertion High Depends on tip size and seal High With safety glasses No conflict Temples can break the seal No conflict Temples can break the seal On a hot floor Comfortable Cups can get hot Comfortable (check the IP rating) Cups can get hot Hearing coworkers Hard without removing them Hard without lifting a cup Hear-through keeps speech audible Hear-through keeps speech audible Easy for a supervisor to check No Yes No Yes Whichever type of hearing protection you choose, the NRR on its package overstates the protection you'll get on the floor. OSHA and NIOSH give you three ways to estimate by how much. Three Ways to Estimate Real-World Protection From an NRR Every hearing protector type mentioned above carries an NRR measured under the Environmental Protection Agency's labeling rule, with trained test subjects and a careful fit. Workers on a plant floor get less than that, so OSHA and NIOSH discount the label using three different methods. For more information on what the number measures, see our article on how NRR ratings work. Method One: OSHA's Appendix B Subtracts 7 dB From the NRR When your noise is measured in dBA, OSHA's Appendix B method tells you to subtract 7 dB from the NRR before you apply it. The 7 dB accounts for the difference between how the NRR is calculated and the A-weighted scale your noise meter reads. Estimated exposure = TWA − (NRR − 7) Method Two: OSHA's 50 Percent Safety Factor Gives a Conservative Planning Number OSHA compliance officers apply a further 50 percent safety factor to the NRR when they decide whether a plant should add engineering controls, which gives you (NRR − 7) ÷ 2. Under a hearing conservation program, OSHA judges your protector with the Appendix B number instead. For your own planning, the halved number becomes a sensible cushion for your measurements. The 50 percent factor leaves room for a rushed fit, a sweaty earmuff seal, and the gap your safety glasses create. Method Three: NIOSH Derates by Protector Type NIOSH recommends subtracting 25 percent of the labeled NRR for earmuffs, 50 percent for slow-recovery foam earplugs and 70 percent for all other earplugs, then applying the 7 dB correction for dBA measurements. The NIOSH method favors earmuffs and discounts most earplugs heavily, which reflects how each type tends to perform in the field. The Three Estimates Side by Side With AXIL Ratings Run AXIL's own ratings through all three methods and the spread is wide: Protector and area OSHA Appendix B (NRR − 7) OSHA 50 percent ((NRR − 7) ÷ 2) NIOSH (derated by type) MX Passive earmuffs, NRR 25, in 95 dBA 77 dBA 86 dBA 83 dBA MX Passive earmuffs, NRR 25, in 100 dBA 82 dBA 91 dBA (over the PEL) 88 dBA GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds with foam tips, NRR 21, in 92 dBA 78 dBA 85 dBA About 88 dBA (foam earplug derate) The same earmuffs can look comfortably safe or over the limit depending on the method they’re measured with. So plan with the conservative number, then make sure your hearing protector is worn correctly, since a poor fit can cost you more protection than the difference between two products' ratings. A fit test goes one step past all three estimates. A fit test measures the protection on your own ears and gives you a Personal Attenuation Rating (PAR). If your hearing conservation program offers fit testing, a PAR is a better guide than any derated label. Derating tends to push buyers toward the highest NRR on the shelf. On a floor at the lower end of the noise range, though, too much protection creates a different hazard. Hearing Overprotection Can Mute Alarms and Speech Hearing overprotection can mute the sounds that keep you safe on the work floor, like a forklift horn, a backup alarm, or a coworker's warning. A worker who can't hear those sounds faces a different kind of injury risk. Overprotection can also lead you to lift an earmuff or pull an earplug every time you need to talk, which removes your hearing protection while the noise is still there. NIOSH advises against overprotection and suggests aiming for just enough reduction to bring your exposure to roughly 75 to 85 dBA. The UK's Health and Safety Executive recommends avoiding protectors that bring the level at your ear below 70 dB. A worked example shows how easy it is to overshoot. Take a foam earplug rated NRR 33 in an 88 dBA area. OSHA's Appendix B method puts your exposure at 88 − 26 = 62 dBA, well below both targets. GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds with foam tips (NRR 21) in that same area land at 74 dBA with Appendix B and 81 dBA with the 50 percent factor, close to or inside NIOSH's range either way. Electronic hear-through also helps at this end of the range. Hear-through lets you choose a moderate NRR and still amplify the sound of alarms and speech that a passive protector would mute. You can learn more in our guide to how electronic hearing protection works. At the top of the noise range, the risk runs the other way. Above 100 dBA, a single protector of any type can leave you short. When to Double Up: Dual Protection Above 100 dBA Double up when your 8-hour TWA tops 100 dBA, the point where NIOSH recommends wearing earplugs and earmuffs together. The 91 dBA result for MX Passive earmuffs in a 100 dBA area shows why a single protector runs out of room there. OSHA's general industry standard doesn't require dual protection. In mining, MSHA requires both an earplug and an earmuff once a miner's TWA exceeds 105 dBA. To estimate your combined protection, the OSHA Technical Manual takes the field-adjusted rating of the higher-rated protector and adds 5 dB. Never add the two NRRs together, because two layers block far less than the sum of their ratings. Here's how much protection doubling up adds for MX Passive earmuffs (NRR 25) worn over GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds with foam tips (NRR 21): Field-adjusted MX Passive rating: (25 − 7) ÷ 2 = 9 dB Add 5 dB for the second layer: 9 + 5 = 14 dB Estimated exposure in a 100 dBA area: 100 − 14 = 86 dBA, back under the PEL In a 105 dBA area, the same pairing estimates 91 dBA. If your work area runs that loud, talk to your safety lead about engineering controls alongside hearing protection equipment. Dual protection only works if you can tolerate both layers for the whole work day. Slim earbuds under an earmuff cushion can feel more comfortable over a long day than bulky foam earplugs under the same earmuffs. Our guide to doubling up with plugs and muffs covers how to wear both layers so each one seals. Two layers also make it harder to hear the people around you, and hearing your coworkers is often the reason protection comes out in the middle of the work day. Industrial Earbuds Let You Hear Coworkers While Protecting Your Hearing On a loud floor, hearing protection often gets pulled off because you need to talk, catch an instruction, or answer a call. NIOSH reports that 28 percent of noise-exposed manufacturing workers say they don't wear hearing protection precisely because they need to hear other sounds during the workday. Hear-Through Keeps Speech and Alarms Audible in Your Earbuds Electronic industrial earbuds let you keep your hearing protection in while you talk. GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds compress sounds above 85 dB and amplify lower-level sounds, like a coworker's voice or a backup alarm, up to 5X. That's AXIL's Protect + Enhance approach on the work floor, and it means the coworker waving at you from two stations down no longer means you have to take an earplug out of your ear. Industrial earbuds handle that need differently from the other three ways workers stay in contact on a floor: Passive protection and raised voices. You'll end up shouting, or lifting your ear protection to hear. Electronic earmuffs. Electronic earmuffs give you the same hear-through, but safety glasses at your temples can break the earmuff seal over a long day. Radio-integrated headsets. A two-way radio is built into the earmuff itself, which suits crews that run everything over the radio. Bluetooth Earbuds Handle Calls Within Plant Rules Bluetooth calling suits supervisors and maintenance staff who move between areas and need to use their phones without removing their hearing protection. GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds limit Bluetooth volume while the hearing enhancement stays on, which keeps a call or music volume at a safer level. Every plant sets its own audio policy, so confirm yours before you rely on Bluetooth. Consumer Noise-Cancelling Earbuds Fall Short of Industrial Protection Consumer noise-cancelling earbuds can look a lot like industrial earbuds, but they belong in a separate category. OSHA says most consumer active noise-cancelling headphones aren't effective for controlling occupational noise, and recommends against using them in place of laboratory-tested protectors . Our article on why noise cancelling is not hearing protection explains the difference. Hearing your coworkers keeps your hearing protection in place, and so does a hearing protector gear that stays comfortable for a 10- or 12-hour day. Comfort, Fit and PPE Compatibility on Long Workdays A Good Seal Has to Hold Up for 10 or 12 Hours Over a long workday, small fit problems add up as your earplugs work loose and your earmuff cushions become warm and soften against your ears. Fit can have a bigger effect on your hearing protection than most spec-sheet differences. The difference between a well-inserted and a poorly inserted earplug can be larger than the difference between two products' NRRs. Tip: With hear-through switched off on your hearing protection, say a few words out loud. Your voice should sound deeper and fuller inside your head when your foam tips are sealed in your ears. If your voice sounds thin, go up a size in your ear tips and reseat them. The tips that come with your hearing protection gear are pre-installed are only a default, so using a different size in each ear is normal. Safety Glasses, Heat and Hard Hats Test Your Seal All Day Safety glasses can break your earmuff’s seal. Each temple arm lifts the earmuff cushion off your skin and lets noise leak in. Thin, flat safety glasses arms at your temples leave the smallest gap, and in-ear protection avoids this problem altogether because there's no cushion for your glasses to lift. On a hot floor, sweat and water resistance are also worth checking on your hearing protection gear. The GS Extreme 3.0, XCOR PRO, and MXII Pro each carry an IP65 rating. AXIL's MX earmuffs use an over-the-head headband. If you wear a hard hat, confirm your hearing protection’s fit with your specific hard hat before spending a full day on the work floor, or pair your hard hat with in-ear protection instead. Battery Life Has to Cover Your Whole Workday Electronic protection only enhances what you hear while the battery lasts. AXIL products have varying runtimes depending on the mode you use: Product Hear-through only Bluetooth only Hear-through plus Bluetooth GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds Up to 40 hours Up to 20 hours Up to 15 hours XCOR PRO earbuds Up to 13 hours Up to 7 hours Up to 5 hours MXII Pro earmuffs About 60 hours About 45 hours About 40 hours MX Pro earmuffs 70 hours 40 hours 30 hours You Can Ask for a Protector That Fits If the hearing protector your plant issues doesn't work for you, say so. OSHA requires employers to let you choose from a variety of suitable hearing protectors, so you're entitled to pick one that fits. AXIL's industrial lineup divides along those same lines: noise level, in-ear or over-ear, and how much hear-through and runtime you need. Matching AXIL Hearing Protection to Plant Floor Noise Levels Matching a hearing protector to your noise level works best with a cautious number. Every estimate here uses OSHA's conservative 50 percent method, so a well-fitted protector should perform better than the figure shown. If your hearing tests have already recorded a drop in your hearing, plan against the 85 dBA target and consider doubling up your hearing protection starting at about 95 dBA. articles.summary: You're on the firing line with your passive earmuffs clamped tight. The range officer calls something down the line, and you catch half of it. You lift one earmuff cup to ask him to repeat it, just as the shooter in the next bay fires and now you’ve got ringing in your ears that you can’t shake off. Electronic earmuffs are built so you never have to lift that cup. Microphones on the outside of each earmuff cup can pick up the sounds around you, and a chip amplifies soft sounds while turning down anything above a set threshold. AXIL's electronic line includes models such as the XCOR, GS Extreme 3.0 and TRACKR, which set that threshold at 85 dB. The sealed earmuff cup provides its rated passive protection the whole time. Electronic earbuds and earplugs work the same way in a smaller housing. Inside a Pair of Electronic Ear Muffs Three components sit inside a pair of electronic earmuffs and let you keep that cup on your ear: the sealed cup itself, a set of outside microphones, and a processor with a small speaker. Sound reaches your ear along two separate paths, and only one of those paths runs through the electronics. The Sealed Earmuff Cup Blocks Sound at All Times Your earmuff cup is the part that protects your hearing. The cup's hard shell and soft cushion seal around your ear and block sound physically, whether the electronics are on or off. Outside Microphones Pick Up the Sound Around You A small microphone on the outside of each earmuff cup picks up softer sounds like range commands, voices, and footsteps. Quality units put one microphone on each side. Two microphones let your brain compare left and right, so you can still tell which direction the sound of a voice or a snapped twig came from. A Processor and Speaker Sit Inside Each Earmuff Cup A chip inside the cup reads the microphone signal and decides how loud each moment of sound should be. A small speaker inside the same cup then plays that sound back to your ear. The chip can raise soft sounds, pass normal sounds through, and turn loud sounds down. Part Where it sits Job Works without power? Sealed cup and cushion Around your ear Blocks sound physically Yes Microphones Outside each cup Pick up outside sound No Processor Inside each cup Sets the playback level No Speaker Inside each cup, facing your ear Plays sound back to you No Electronic earbuds and electronic earplugs carry the same parts in a smaller housing, with the ear tip doing the sealing. Read more about how to fit electronic ear plugs so that tip seals properly in our guide. Of those parts, the processor decides what reaches your ear when a shot goes off. Compression vs Clipping: What Happens When a Shot Goes Off When a shot goes off, the processor inside your earmuff cup either compresses the sound or clips it. You’ll experience the difference in what you hear during the shot and in the second right after it. Before the Shot, Soft Sounds Get Amplified Up to the moment the shot breaks, the processor amplifies sound below its threshold. AXIL offers up to 5X hearing enhancement on the GS Extreme 3.0 and the MXII Pro, with adjustable levels so you can choose how much boost you hear. Softer sounds like a range officer's command or a hunting partner's whisper can come through louder than you'd hear it with bare ears. Compression Turns the Shot Down and Keeps Voices Coming Through Once the shot crosses the threshold, a compression circuit turns the playback down to a safe level. The XCOR, GS Extreme 3.0 and TRACKR set that threshold at 85 dB. NIOSH uses the same number for its recommended exposure limit, 85 dBA averaged over an eight-hour workday. Our decibel guide explains why 85 dB is the line where protection starts. A compression circuit keeps passing sound through the shot at that lower volume, so a command spoken over the shot still reaches you. Clipping Cuts Your Hearing Off for a Moment Older and cheaper circuits clip loud sounds instead of compressing. A clipping circuit cuts the microphones entirely when the shot arrives, so you hear a moment of silence before sound returns. If your range partner was talking when the shot broke, you can lose the next few words.
